translations.text: Bricín of Tuaim Drecon was, after the Lent of the great Passion, on Easter night,
unable [?] to go from the abbot's house to the church, and [this was through] weakness [?], so that he heard the cry of the household of heaven celebrating Easter.
It was then that Bricín said: 'O my Lord, if it is right in your sight, send me from you a righteous messenger with tidings of your kingdom.'
After that the angel of the Lord came to speak with him between midnight and matins.
He touched [?] the tip of each of his fingers, so that the world was laid open to his eye, and he saw the multitudes of the household of heaven around the heavenly altar.
'Good, then,' said Bricín, 'for God has granted [?] me my prayer.'
Let me learn from you of every godly Christian raising-up [?] that will take place in building the church of God until the end of the world.'
'Good indeed,' said the angel,
'a third of the millennium we are in is left until the end; and moreover seven years will be taken off your own life because of the request you have made,
and moreover you will not go to heaven, and the [?] will not go [?] into your body until you have died; and the house you are in will endure as long as the faith lasts in Ireland.
And moreover, know that the number of psalms you had sung before I came to you
is the number of [?] that there will be over Ireland, that is, from 'Beatus vir' to 'Miserere mei Deus quoniam conculcavit.''
'A question, then, O blessed one,' said Bricín to the angel:
'which son of life comes first of them here at the beginning? Tell me fully!'
'Good indeed,' said the angel, 'there will be a time when a land will be given [?] to foreigners, which will let fall [?] candle-speckled [?] [?] when it is shown [?]
[?] towards a half-grave [?]; heads of hair will be brought about faces [?] [?] towards a half-empty grave, for hosts would gather to [?] a great clamour [?].
After that there will be vengeance with persecution against the churches of God, so that many will all be [?] of Máel Brigte.'
'There will be after him,' said the angel,
'the prince of the three fair [?] monasteries, the shrine [?] of the Conaille, of a many-formed race, who will make fruitful [?] dwellings round about,
who will build [?] adorned churches round about; he will be a sage, he will be a king, he will be a bishop, he will be full of almsgiving and mercy.
Twelve years until his first departure.' 'That is the mercy of God,' said Bricín.
'There will then be the destroyer, for sixty-eight [?] from Loch Gamenais in the north, whose [?] is this,
who will turn his black into white, namely Tanaide son of Uidir.' 'That is the mercy of God.'
'There will then be the smiter, who will [?] against the world for the space of seventeen hundred [?],
until he goes to death by weapons, together with his very mighty war-band, by very rough spear-points, in the raids [?] of Clúain.'
'That is mercy,' said Bricín. 'A blessing on [?]!'
'There will also be [?] the pious [?]. His rule will not change for six score
years. He will be both of God and a man.' 'That is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] from the green who will sow gospels to cattle and to peoples with red buildings, for three years and three score.'
'That is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] of the two meadows, that is, Clonard and Clonmacnoise, for three years and eighty.
He will be both of God and a man. He will be a demon who will make little of much and much of little.
That [?] of two halves.' 'That is great mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the long-sided [?], slender, bent, red one between Droing and Uisnech for five years and eighty.
Many will be honoured according to the breadth of his company. His rule will be mottled; it will be a net for small fish and big fish.'
'That is the King's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the clean-handed one of Mainistir (Monasterboice) for nine months and ninety. His [?] will spread across the sea.
He will be the crystal gem [?] of the dragon stone.' 'It is merciful,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] black-curled [?] of the seat of Comgall (Bangor) for a year and fifty.
He will not give power over [?] of the earth [?].'
'There will also be the trembling-headed one of Loch Con for seven years and three score; he will hold [?], he will scatter [?] like ashes [?].'
'That is great mercy from the King,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] of Slieve Fuait, with a monastic rule, with a martyr's devotion, with the benefit of litanies, with [?] of his soul-friend.'
'That is great mercy from the King,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the slow-[?], thick-[?] one from Domnach for four score years.
He will [?] laws upon red-sided [?]; he will make peace with [?].' 'That is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] of Lough Ree, whom the three choirs will sing, that is, the choir of Munster, the choir of Connacht, and the choir of the Uí Néill.
The music of the three seats, that is, the seat of Ciarán, of Commán and of Crónán.
Nineteen years and fifty will be his age.' 'That is mercy from God,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the half-bronze moon of the west of Armagh, that is, shining in piety.
"And the rule will be his for sixty years. His herds of horses and his chariots will be great. A good [?] for the churches of the Christians."
"There will also be the crooked-horned [?] [?] one from Slieve Gullion for seven [?] before [?], who is in the shape of a cow of every herd [?]."
"That is a mercy from God," said Bricín.
"There will also be the speckled-faced, sweet-[?] one from Loch Erne for the space of eight months, with authority. He will enrich old and young warriors alike; he will make smooth what is rough."
"There will also be the red-feathered one of Inis Muiredaig for nine periods [?] and sixty years.
Foreigners will drive [?] him from the islands. Three showers will be poured out [?] in his time [?]: that is, a shower of rain and a shower of hail [?] on the middle of Mag Corainn."
"The righteous God is merciful," said Bricín.
"There will also be the renowned one of Cluain Eois for eighty years. He will fill Armagh with great treasures.
He will tread [?] the roads of Ireland with herds of horses and with chariots; he will [?] with covenants and laws."
"It is a great mercy," said Bricín.
"There will also be the fork-mouthed one of Dún Lethglaise.
He will [?] between Ros and Rinn for six months and a hundred years; he will [?], for the sea is not ventured upon [?]; sweeter than harps [?]."
"There will also be the board-faced one of Glenn Gemin for ten years.
He will disturb every very deep law. He will be terrible against evils; he will [?] everyone."
"There will also be the little [?] one of Benn Codail for the space of ten years.
He will be as blossoming as flowers and as rough as blackthorn." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"There will also be the long-sided one of Tech Telli for forty years.
He will fill mills and plough-teams and horses and vessels and kitchens." "That is the mercy of God," said Bricín.
"There will also be the fork-headed one of Cell Daigri for sixty years: a rough, pious, pure, unlearned man.
He will see [?] three splendours: the splendour of the fair of Tailtiu, the splendour of the law at Uisnech, and the splendour of the great battles of Ireland at Mag Léna."
"It is the mercy of God," said Bricín.
"There will also be the slender-[?] one of Slemain for ninety years.
He will be abbot of the three [?], monk of the three rules, [?] of the three seats [?]." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"There will also be the brown-faced one from Aiche, who will be suited to every law, both good and evil,
with the face of a holy dove, the heart of a hawk, and the strength of a bull." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the white [?] one of Clonkeen for three score years.
He will be a prophet of the abundance [?] of the territories; he will make a free tribute out of servitude [?]." "Even so, it is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the black beetle of Druim Tibrud for forty years and forty months.
He will honour justice, he will [?] the freedom of the church, he will sow the gospels." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the upturned-head [?] of Movilla for a day and a month and a year and seventy years.
His assemblies will be slow, his vengeances will be swift, his punishments will be fierce." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the deaf one of Cloon or of Cúil Conáin for seven score
years. Clever will be his time as a servant-boy, gentle his manhood, charitable his old age."
"Then there will be the branch-grey one from Lusk for thirty years.
He will win [?] the three bonds [?], that is, the bond of piety, the bond of wisdom, the bond of good management." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the rough-cloaked [?] one of the Slige Midlúachra for nine years.
Bloody and wooded [?]; weak the beginning of his rule, strong and speckled [?] its middle, strong its end."
"It is a mercy from my Lord," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the little stony [?] one from Brí Léith, who will follow the rule of the Romans for seven score years; he will both preserve and destroy."
"It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the winter-madman of Derry (Daire Calgaig), who will take the kingship of Conall three times, for thirty-three years.
He will leave the Foyle under noble, fair-weathered headlands [?]. His rule will be a bridge [?] between Ireland and Scotland." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the frenzied [?] one of Tulach Tuirbe for three score
years: a palm here, a hand with another [?]; a leap into heaven, a leap into earth." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
"Then there will be the red-backed [?] one of Roscam for seventy years.
He is the bronze stone above the lake of new milk. He will brighten every wood [?]." "It is a mercy," said Bricín.
Then there will be the toothed [?] one of Derry, as this poem says:
The toothed [?] one of Derry will [?] for a time on the shores of Loch Dá Dael; from Loch Dá Dael it is quickly [?] that he will dwell in Lochán Eidin.
From Loch Eidin on the flood toward the [?] after that; though afterwards he will meet with it from Lusk to Devenish.
From Cruach meic Dara under pledge [?], after Colum of Derry (Daire Calgaig), for three nights [?] the feast of a king [?] ... [?] the shrine [?]. The sage, the bishop,

…and a king who will bring peace and law to Macha (Armagh). He will come from the north, from Dún Bó [?]. The treasures of Ireland and Scotland will be his. A gathering from the sea will be brought to him in the estuary of Swords on the night of [?].
There will be gold, there will be silver, there will be crystal, there will be wine in ships from the Romans. On an unwarlike day [?] Dá Del [?]; though it is welcome, it is not well come [?].
Welcome to the people of bright piety; not welcome from the wicked. A .iiii. [?]
Ten oxen of Mugna will be brought as its [?]. Between Rinn and Ros there will be a gathering of tears and wringing of hands.
Afterwards he will fall in a cemetery on a Tuesday after the Sacrifice (the Mass). His remains will be carried to Iona, where the relics of Ségéne are.
He will be five years short of a hundred when he passes on and goes to his death.
'The noble offspring of the family is a great mercy from our Lord.'
'There will also be the stone [?] of ice (that is, Flann) above the fiery embers in Fore.
Gentle will be his appearance and his clerical life, yet he will be burned [?] around the world for eighty years.' 'It is a mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the bloody hewer [?] of Clonfad. He will make the dark and the rough straight.
He will be a servant of the monastic life. He will be generous in alms to the multitude. He will be of God, he will be a man [?].' 'It is a mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the roarer of Fahan Mura (that is, Fothad of the Canon) for ninety years.
He has [?] the three gifts, that is, the gift of learning, the gift of wisdom, and the gift of chastity.'
'There will also be the true, troubled [?] well in the green of Slane for sixty-one years.
He will be fasting, keeping three-day fasts, and generous at one time, and [?] at the other time.' 'It is the mercy of God,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the priest, the presbyter of Tuaim Fobair, for eighty years.
He will bless everyone, and everyone will be blessing him. He will reach out [?] to everyone, and everyone will reach toward [?] him.
He will give to everyone, and everyone will be giving to him.' 'It is the mercy of God,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the dwarf of Mag Belaig for sixty-seven years.
He will be the wine-blossom side by side with what is unlike it, that is, a candle of piety out of a well of sin.
He will be the single [?] remnant of the plunder that the devil seized long ago.'
'There will also be the cold-girdled one from Devenish, the slender, delicate one, for a year.
He will not be a lax companion [?]. He will give up his own will for the sake of reward. Many assemblies [?] will not change him [?].' 'It is the mercy of God,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the offered rib from Cell ar Loch for fifty years and six months. He will offer the nobility of his race on the path [?] of humility;
he will run down into a valley on the [?] of his soul, so that his true humility raised up his nobility [?].'
'That is God's mercy; that is the makings of a virgin,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the long-sided [?] faster of Connor, for thirty-seven years.
His mind will be virginal and he will be devoted to God, since he will be generous and giving to people.' 'It is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the whisperer [?counsellor] of Áth Blair, for forty-one years.
He will take the hostages of Connacht for three years and a month.' 'It is merciful.'
'There will also be the rough one of Glenn Gemin (that is, Dúnchad úa Bruin), who will establish [?] the three ordinances [?], that is,
the ordinance [?] of Adomnán and of Ségéne and of Colum Cille, for seventy-nine periods [?].'
'That is mercy from God,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] of Suide Chaim, that is, he whose [?] will give certain tidings of the future.
He will soften hard hearts by recounting the demons and the things of hell, for eight score [years].' 'It is merciful,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the golden head on the iron column in Clonard, that is, a radiant face on a troubled [?] column, for nine
years three times over, with wisdom, with virginity, with rule.' 'It is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the high praiser of truth of Inis Cloitgi, for forty-four years.
He will be the white-bronze cup on the lead cross, that is, a description of profit coming out of unprofitableness [?].
He will rebuke the wicked.' 'It is merciful,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the slender [?] of Tulach Én, for thirty-seven years. He will be [?]; he will be force, great force [?].
His hollow breast will be a [?inheritance]; he will be guileless from the heart; he will be unsteady [?].' 'It is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the [?] of Armagh. His morning will be early, his noon will be long.
He will be a half-grown side [?], he will be a half-cold [?], he will be a mingled flame;
he will burn law and lawlessness alike, through the severity of his piety and the weakness of his wisdom.' 'It is God's mercy,' said Bricín.
'There will also be the poor man who will preach, for thirty-three years.
There will also be the white well [?] who will bring peace to the borders of Ireland.
It is he who will put a lock of [?] on the [?] of Ireland, and that is the end of the faith and the Christianity of the world.' 'It is all great,' said Bricín.
In the time of Áed Engach Tibraite will be born, says Baile in Scáil (The Phantom's Frenzy).
'And what will there be then?' said Bricín.
"A remembrance of the faith of Antichrist," said the angel.
"It would be a mercy of God," said Bricín, "if the people of this island did not come to that."
"They will not come to it indeed," said the angel, "for on the Cruach [Croagh Patrick] God granted Patrick these four things, namely:
that there should be no lack of learning in Ireland until the end of the world; and that foreigners should not inhabit Ireland, whether by consent or by force, until Doomsday;
and that the sea should cover Ireland seven years before Doomsday; and that he himself should be judge over the Irish on the Day of Judgement."
"Thanks be to God," said Bricín.
"Amen," said the angel.
